Mr. Sk. Md. Mr. Abdul Quayum with Morshed ------ For the petitioner. 
Mr. Md. Omar Faruque ------ For the opposite parties.
parties:
Mosammat Rehana Akhter
Vs.
Rizia Begum and others
full_judgment:
The preemptor opposite party No. 1 filed Preemption Miscellaneous Case No. 5 of 2002 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Mirsarai Sadar, Chittagong, under Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act for preemption of the case land, stating, in short that the total land under B.S. khatian No. 1196 belonged to Jabeda Khatun, Md. Yeasin, Foyez Ahmad and Aslam Miah; the said Jobeda Khatun sold out her portion to Fakir Ahmad that said Yeasin died leaving behind a wife, sons, namely, Shabuddin, Ruhul Amin, Md. Azim Uddin, Md. Tajul Islam and Zafor Ahmad; that said Ruhul Amin, Md. Azim Uddin, Zafor Ahmad and wife of Yeasin and her daughter sold out their portion to opposite party No. 4, Sudhir Chandra Sharma; that the said Foyez Amed died leaving behind the opposite parties Nos. 5 to 10 and the preemptor Rizia Begum; that said Aslam Miah gifted his portion to opposite parties Nos. 13 to 15; that the seller Fakir Ahmed had no other land in the khatian after the sale in question and as such he was not made a party to the case; that the seller without any notice to the preemptor sold out the land in question to the preemptee-opposite party-petitioner and the preemptor came to know the same on 24.01.2002; that the preemptor is a co-sharer by inheritance in the khatian and the preemptee is a stranger to the khatian in question and as such she is entitled to get the land in question by preemption. 

 12. Now the main question is whether in preemption proceeding the Court can consider the correctness of the disputed khatian in order to see whether the preemptors or his predecessor's name has been correctly recorded in the disputed khatian. It appears the preemptee in his written objection specifically stated that the disputed khatian published in the name of Foiz Ahmed predecessor of the preemptor was wrong in as much as Foiz Ahmed had no subsisting interest in the land of the khatian while the said khatian was recorded in his name. To substantiate this fact the preemptee specifically stated this fact in her written objection as well as in the deposition of O.P.W.1 her husband Nazrul Islam. The preemptee also cross-examined the P.W.1 preemptor on this point that the disputed khatian was wrongly printed in the name of Foiz Ahmed having no subsisting interest in the land of the khatian. It appears both the Courts held that in a pre-emption proceedings this kind of complicated question cannot be decided which can only be decided in a properly constituted civil suit. Mr. Abdul Quayum in support of his submission that in a preemption proceeding this kind of question about correctness of the khatian and correctness of the mutation proceeding and other similar maters can be considered has referred to the decision in the case of Kutu Chand Miah-Vs-Rabindra Kumar Deb and others reported in 22 DLR 29 and the decision of Md. Khairullah Bhuiyan-Vs- Haji Nurul Alam Chowdhury, being dead his heirs Amena Khatun and others reported in 35 DLR (AD) 338. On perusal of the 1st decision which has been reported in 22 DLR 294 it appears in the said decision it has been held that in a proceeding under Section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act the correctness of the record of right can be inquired into and held that the recording of the applicants name in the record of right was not correct and accordingly the trial Court rejected the application for preemption, which was upheld by the High Court. Similarly in the 2nd decision reported in 35 DLR 338 it has been held that the order of Revenue Officer splitting up a joint-tenancy in whichever way it may be designed, if it severs the old relationship of the co-sharers and thereby destroys a co-sharer's statutory right of preemption, cannot be examined by the Court in a preemption proceeding in order to be satisfied that prima-facie the order was passed in accordance with law, that is to say, whether the mandatory provisions of section 117(e) of the E.B.S.A. and Tenancy Act were complied with on the face of the record. In the said decision it was further held:- "The scope of this examination cannot be so limited as to ask the Court to keep its eyes closed and to accept without hesitation whatever order is placed before it, simply because the order was passed by a competent Revenue Officer."
